\chapter{Answering With More Than Yes}
\label{ch:ka-replies}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer in Kannada with more than yes and no --- true, enough, certainly, perhaps, just so --- and see the three-vowel grid running under \kn{ಇದು}, \kn{ಅದು} and \kn{ಹೇಗೆ}.}

Complete KA-C49-just-so and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nija]{\kn{ನಿಜ} (nija) — true}

\label{lesson:KA-C49-true}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{atithi} mean, and what did \emph{raita} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನಿಜ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನಿಜ}} (\emph{nija}) — \textquotedblleft{}true\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{nija} began as 'one's own, innate, born in' — what belongs to a thing by nature rather than by accident.

Kannada and Telugu both took that and turned it toward truth, and you can watch the turn happen inside the word: what is true of a thing is what the thing is in itself, as against what is merely said about it. Said alone, \kn{ನಿಜ} does the work of a whole sentence — 'true', 'that's right'.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five replies that do more than agree or refuse.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nija}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nija}, then \emph{haudu}, and hear how much more the first one claims
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ನಿಜ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}true\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sāku]{\kn{ಸಾಕು} (sāku) — enough}

\label{lesson:KA-C49-enough}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nija} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಸಾಕು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಸಾಕು}} (\emph{sāku}) — \textquotedblleft{}enough\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಸಾಕು} is a complete sentence with one word in it. Held up over a plate while someone is ladling rice, it means 'that's enough' and stops the ladle.

No Sanskrit anywhere in it — \kn{ಸಾಕು} is Kannada's own, resting on an inherited verb for sufficing. It covers a whole English shelf on its own: enough, plenty, stop, that will do. Kannada is content to let the situation and the tone sort out which.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: true, and enough.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sāku}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sāku} over an imaginary plate, then \emph{nija} to something just said
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಸಾಕು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}enough\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khaṇḍita]{\kn{ಖಂಡಿತ} (khaṇḍita) — certainly}

\label{lesson:KA-C49-certainly}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sāku} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಖಂಡಿತ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಖಂಡಿತ}} (\emph{khaṇḍita}) — \textquotedblleft{}certainly\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{khaṇḍita} means 'broken, cut off' — a piece severed from the rest.

The road from there to 'certainly' is worth walking. A matter that has been cut is a matter that has been settled: nothing left hanging, no remainder to argue over. English does the very same thing with \emph{decide}, which is Latin for cutting off, and with a \emph{clear-cut} answer. Two languages, no contact between them, one metaphor.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: true, enough, certainly.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{khaṇḍita}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{khaṇḍita} as an answer to an invitation, then \emph{nija} as an answer to a claim
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಖಂಡಿತ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}certainly\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bahuśaḥ]{\kn{ಬಹುಶಃ} (bahuśaḥ) — perhaps}

\label{lesson:KA-C49-perhaps}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{khaṇḍita} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬಹುಶಃ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬಹುಶಃ}} (\emph{bahuśaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}perhaps\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{bahuśas}, 'in many ways, in many instances', from \emph{bahu}, 'much, many'. If a thing can fall out in many ways then no one of them is settled, and the word slid quietly from 'in many ways' to 'probably, perhaps'. It is the exact opposite journey to the one \kn{ಖಂಡಿತ} took.

Notice the last mark: \kn{ಃ}, the \emph{visarga}, a light breath let out at the end of a word. It is uncommon in everyday Kannada, and this is one of the few ordinary words that carries it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the fourth one takes back what the third one promised.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bahuśaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{khaṇḍita}, then \emph{bahuśaḥ}, and hear the certainty drain out
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬಹುಶಃ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}perhaps\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hāge]{\kn{ಹಾಗೆ} (hāge) — that way, just so}

\label{lesson:KA-C49-just-so}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bahuśaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹಾಗೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹಾಗೆ}} (\emph{hāge}) — \textquotedblleft{}that way, just so\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಹಾಗೆ} means 'that way, like that', and offered on its own it agrees: 'just so'. \kn{ಹಾಗೇ} \kn{ಆಗಲಿ} — let it be that way.

Now set it beside \kn{ಹೇಗೆ}, the question word for 'how' that this book gave you early on. They differ in one vowel. Supply the third and the shape is complete:

\kn{ಹೀಗೆ} — this way. \kn{ಹಾಗೆ} — that way. \kn{ಹೇಗೆ} — which way?

That is the same three-way grid as \kn{ಇದು}, \kn{ಅದು} and \kn{ಎಲ್ಲಿ}: \kn{ಇ}- for what is near, \kn{ಅ}- for what is away, \kn{ಎ}- for what is being asked about. Kannada builds a great many of its small words on those three vowels, and once you can hear them you stop learning such words one at a time.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five replies: true, enough, certainly, perhaps, just so.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hāge}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{hīge}, \emph{hāge}, \emph{hēge} as one run
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಹಾಗೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}that way, just so\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
